claim: The obesity cohort consists of 126 healthy volunteers (63 males and 63 females without atherosclerosis and diabetes), all are older adults (range from 53 to 78 years) who are either overweight or obese (BMI >27).
source: The 300-OB cohort includes 126 healthy volunteers (63 males and 63 females without atherosclerosis and diabetes), all are older adults (range from 53 to 78 years) who are either overweight or obese (BMI >27). This healthy cohort of 126 individuals is referred to as the 'obesity cohort' (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the composition and characteristics of the obesity cohort, including sample size, gender distribution, age range, and BMI criteria.

claim: The normal BMI cohort consists of 473 healthy individuals (202 males and 271 females) of Caucasian origin, with 82% of individuals younger than 30 and the majority (388 individuals) in the normal BMI range (18–25).
source: We further used the 500-FG cohort (Ter Horst et al., 2016), which includes 473 healthy individuals (202 males and 271 females) of Caucasian origin. The individuals range from 18 to 75 years of age with 82% of individuals younger than 30. Individuals had BMIs ranging from 15 to 35 with the majority (388 individuals) in the normal BMI range (18–25).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the composition and characteristics of the normal BMI cohort, citing the source study (Ter Horst et al., 2016).

claim: The two-dimensional map of parameters describes 80% of the variability in clinical and physiological parameters in the obesity cohort.
source: Applying this construction on the obesity cohort yielded a two-dimensional map that could describe a large part of the variability (80%) in clinical and physiological parameters.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of variability explained by the two-dimensional map based on analysis of the obesity cohort data.

claim: Proximal parameters in the map are positively correlated and parameters located in opposite sides of the map are negatively correlated.
source: The circular organization of the map reflects a relatively simple structure of interrelations among parameters: proximal parameters are positively correlated and parameters that are located in opposite sides of the map are negatively correlated (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D, and Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the correlation structure of the map and references supporting figures showing examples of these correlations.

claim: Glucose and triglycerides parameters are positively correlated with 23% correlation of measured levels.
source: For instance, as demonstrated in Figure 1B, the proximal glucose and triglycerides parameters are positively correlated (23% correlation of measured levels), and two parameters located in opposing sides of the map – adiponectin and liver fat – are negatively correlated (43% anti-correlation of measured levels).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correlation value between glucose and triglycerides and references Figure 1B showing this relationship.

claim: Adiponectin and liver fat are negatively correlated with 43% anti-correlation of measured levels.
source: For instance, as demonstrated in Figure 1B, the proximal glucose and triglycerides parameters are positively correlated (23% correlation of measured levels), and two parameters located in opposing sides of the map – adiponectin and liver fat – are negatively correlated (43% anti-correlation of measured levels).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the anti-correlation value between adiponectin and liver fat and references Figure 1B showing this relationship.

claim: The positions of parameters in the map of the obesity cohort are similar to the positions of parameters in a map constructed using the normal-BMI cohort.
source: We confirmed that the positions of parameters in the map of the obesity cohort are similar to the positions of parameters in a map that was constructed using the normal-BMI cohort (Figure 1C, left), despite major differences in age and BMI ranges (see details of the normal-BMI map in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the similarity between maps from different cohorts and references Figure 1C showing this comparison.

claim: The map is consistent in separate analyses of males and females.
source: In addition, the map is also consistent in separate analyses of males and females (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the consistency of the map across gender-specific analyses and references Figure 1C showing this comparison.

claim: Lipoproteins span the entire boundary of the circle in the map.
source: We noted a different distribution of each category: lipoproteins span the entire boundary of the circle, hemodynamic parameters are primarily localized at the top-right edge of the circle, metabolic parameters are localized in two defined regions (on the left and top-right sides of the circle), and immunological parameters do not have specific localization (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the distribution of lipoproteins in the map and references Figure 1D showing this distribution.

claim: Hemodynamic parameters are primarily localized at the top-right edge of the circle in the map.
source: We noted a different distribution of each category: lipoproteins span the entire boundary of the circle, hemodynamic parameters are primarily localized at the top-right edge of the circle, metabolic parameters are localized in two defined regions (on the left and top-right sides of the circle), and immunological parameters do not have specific localization (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the distribution of hemodynamic parameters in the map and references Figure 1D showing this distribution.

claim: Metabolic parameters are localized in two defined regions (on the left and top-right sides of the circle) in the map.

claim: For each of the particular measures in the endogenous lipoprotein pathway, there is a clear correspondence between the order of subfractions along the known endogenous pathway and the anticlockwise order of parameters along the map.
source: We found that for each of the particular measures, there is a clear correspondence between the order of subfractions along the known endogenous pathway and the anticlockwise order of parameters along the map (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C), indicating that the circle reflects gradual changes in the maturation of lipoproteins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the correspondence between lipoprotein subfraction order and map position, and references Figure 1E showing this relationship.

claim: In 91% of the individuals from the two healthy cohorts, there is a global gradient of measurements over the map.
source: Surprisingly, in 91% of the individuals from the two healthy cohorts, we found a global gradient of measurements over the map: in each individual, the measured levels varied from negative (i.e., lower than average) values in one side of the map to positive (i.e., higher than average) values in the opposite side of the map (e.g., obese individuals #1–8 in Figure 2A and normal-BMI individuals #9–18 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of individuals showing a global gradient and references figures showing examples.

claim: For 9% of the individuals, there were no major differences in measured levels between the two opposing sides of the map (balanced state).
source: For 9% of the individuals, there were no major differences in measured levels between the two opposing sides of the map – that is, these individuals are in a 'balanced state' without any observed gradient (e.g., individuals #19 and #20 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of individuals in a balanced state and references a figure showing examples.

claim: The IM1 state explains 25% (on average) of the variation among obese individuals.
source: Consistent with this notion, the two states indeed have similar contribution to phenotypic diversity: whereas the IM1 state explains 25% (on average) of the variation among obese individuals, the IM2 state explains, on average, additional 25% of this variation (Figure 2B); similarly, the IM1 and IM2 states explain 20% and 28% of the variation among normal-BMI individuals, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage of variation explained by the IM1 state in the obesity cohort and references Figure 2B.

claim: The IM2 state explains, on average, additional 25% of the variation among obese individuals.

source: Interestingly, IM2 is associated with cytokine responses to all four bacterial stimulations but not to the fungal stimulation (C. albicans; Figure 3B).

claim: Most associations with clinical parameters reflect the association with the whole-body state.
source: This analysis confirmed that most associations with clinical parameters reflect the association with the whole-body state: (i) although the map of parameters was constructed using only healthy individuals, we observed global gradients over the map for the conventional associations between each clinical parameter and disease (Figure 5C, left), which is in agreement with the direction of associations of each disease with the IM1 and IM2 states (Figure 5A,B), and (ii) accounting for the state drastically reduced the number of significant associations (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes that most parameter-disease associations reflect the whole-body state based on the analysis showing reduced associations when accounting for the state.

claim: Both IM1 and IM2 relate to clinical parameters with a known causal role in atherosclerosis.
source: We found a role for both IM1 and IM2 in atherosclerosis, and hence in CVD. First, both IM1 and IM2 relate to clinical parameters with a known causal role in atherosclerosis: out of two known causal atherosclerosis factors (Ference et al., 2017; Nordestgaard, 2016), one is located nearby the most extreme point of the IM1 axis (the percentage of triglyceride in VLDL-remnants [also called 'IDLs']) and one is located nearby the most extreme point of the IM2 axis (LDL cholesterol; Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that both IM1 and IM2 relate to known causal atherosclerosis factors, citing Ference et al., 2017 and Nordestgaard, 2016, and references Figure 6A.

claim: The percentage of triglyceride in VLDL-remnants (IDLs) is a known causal atherosclerosis factor located near the most extreme point of the IM1 axis.
